prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many atoms are held in a magic-wavelength trap, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single part, B009, to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After reading all eight statements the case looks stronger to me on the physics, not because of the count (all eight now prefer it, and I do not treat that as evidence). The new element is specific. A lattice operated at the magic wavelength cancels the differential light shift to first order, so thousands of atoms are interrogated simultaneously in the Lamb-Dicke regime, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, with a signal-to-noise ratio and averaging time that a single trapped ion cannot match. That is a different principle from the frequency comb (a ruler for optical frequencies) and from the 2012 ion work (control of one quantum system at a time). The experimental record is the kind I trust: Sr, Yb and Hg lattice clocks in several laboratories are compared directly and agree at the 1e-18 level, the systematics budgets (blackbody radiation, lattice hyperpolarizability, collisional shifts) have been worked through independently, and the same instruments then gave results that are physics in their own right, namely millimetre-scale gravitational redshift across a sample, spin-exchange and many-body effects in a lattice, and bounds on constant drift. On credit, Katori's 2003 magic-wavelength proposal and the RIKEN demonstration of a Sr lattice clock, together with the JILA programme that took it from the 1e-16 to the 1e-18 regime and understood why the many-atom system behaves as it does, form a natural and defensible pair. I would word the citation around the lattice principle and not around the number 1e-18, which answers the 'lifetime achievement' and 'better numbers' objections raised by Olsson, Danielsson and Eriksson.
statement.case_against: The reservations I take seriously are three. First, overlap: the 2005 prize (comb) and 2012 prize (single-ion control and the Al+ clock) cover neighbouring ground, and the lattice clock reads out through a comb and borrows ion-clock ideas such as clock comparison and quantum-logic thinking. If the committee decides that the citation cannot make the magic-wavelength lattice stand apart, then B009 is weakened. Second, priority: the RIKEN, JILA, SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups all contributed essential early demonstrations, and I am still working partly from memory on exactly who first reached which accuracy level and who first showed the Sr lattice clock beyond the microwave Cs standard. Third, maturity: the redefinition of the second, the relativistic-geodesy applications and the dark-matter searches are not yet realised, so they should be described as what the instrument makes possible and not as part of the prize reasoning. None of the three is decisive for me. The first is answered by the citation, the second is a task for the outside evaluation the Secretary has proposed, and the third is simply a reason not to lean on prospective impact.

responses.point: Danielsson says that I was too quick to claim no overlap with the 2005 comb prize, because the lattice clock relies on the comb for frequency readout, and that the citation must name the magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms and not accuracy.
responses.response: I accept the correction. In round 1 I said the comb prize recognised the ruler and the lattice clock is a different principle, which is true of the principle, but it is not true that the two are independent in practice: every optical clock comparison to the microwave standard goes through a comb. I would put it this way: the comb makes any optical clock usable, and the lattice clock is what makes an optical clock both accurate and statistically fast. That is a dependency, not an overlap in the invention being credited. I therefore support wording that names the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation, with no accuracy figure in the citation, and I agree with you that the Secretary should still ask outside reviewers to confirm the lineage.

responses.point: Eriksson says he is less relaxed than I am about the 2012 ion-clock prize, since it covers some of the same ground on clock accuracy, and that the citation must rest on the lattice concept and many-atom interrogation.
responses.response: I take the 2012 point more seriously than I did in round 1. The Al+ clock of Wineland's group is a clock-accuracy result and a reader could see the lattice clock as the neutral-atom continuation of it. My reply is that the two routes face opposite limits. An ion clock has almost no systematic perturbation from the trap, but it is limited by one ion's signal and so by averaging time. The lattice clock accepts a trap and cancels its effect at the magic wavelength, in exchange for orders of magnitude more atoms, which is why it reaches 1e-18 in hours and not weeks. That trade is the invention. It also gave a new class of physics (many-body interactions in a clock) that no single-ion clock can show. If the committee agrees, the citation should state the many-atom magic-wavelength element and omit clock accuracy as such, as you suggest. If it does not, then the overlap with 2012 is a real argument against B009 and I would want to hear what evidence would resolve it.

responses.point: Pearce, as Chair, asks whether Jun Ye's decisive contribution is the lattice clock itself or the wider JILA programme, and whether Hall's earlier role bears on how Ye's share is framed.
responses.response: I would answer from the laboratory side. Ye's decisive contribution is the lattice clock, and not the wider programme: the Sr lattice clock at JILA is where the magic-wavelength scheme was taken from the first demonstrations to the 1e-18 regime, through the control of lattice light shifts, blackbody radiation and collisional effects, and then to the observation of many-body spin-exchange physics in the same instrument. Those are results on the lattice clock, not on comb spectroscopy in general. Hall's role does not weaken the share: Hall was honoured for the comb, while the lattice work is a separate programme in which Ye led the experiments. As I disclosed, I spent a year of my PhD in Hall's lab, and I flag that again for the record. It was long ago and it is not a tie to Ye, so I do not regard it as a reason for me to step back, but the committee should decide that and not I.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the credit rests on Katori's proposal and first demonstration or also on Ye's accuracy and stability milestones, and wants the history checked, noting that I share the memory gap.
responses.response: I agree that the record must be checked and I would not finalise without it. My working reading, to be tested: Katori and collaborators supplied the magic-wavelength proposal (2003) and the RIKEN Sr lattice-clock demonstration, and the JILA group then provided the accuracy and stability milestones and the many-body measurements. These are two distinct contributions in different phases, which is the standard structure for a shared prize and is separable in the way you ask for. Lemonde (SYRTE), Takamoto, Ludlow and Oates (NIST) and PTB were important, but each is on one side of that line, either an early realisation that Katori's name already covers in the RIKEN work or an independent reproduction and improvement. If the outside evaluation finds that another name is essential to the first demonstration, I would want the committee to reconsider, and the three-name limit would allow one more name. At present I do not see that evidence.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that a citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation separates B009 from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.

The exact priority sequence among RIKEN, JILA, SYRTE, PTB and NIST for the first Sr lattice clock and for the 1e-16 and 1e-18 milestones, which I am still partly recalling from memory and which the outside evaluation should confirm.
Whether Takamoto or another early RIKEN or JILA contributor would be judged essential, in which case a third name could be added within the limit.
Whether the redefinition of the second and the new-physics searches will be read as realised impact; I would keep them out of the citation.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict specific to B009. For the record: I spent a year of my PhD in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, a loose and long-past link to the JILA environment of Jun Ye, which I do not regard as disqualifying and leave to the committee to judge. I am on the management team of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (Chalmers-led, centred on superconducting qubits), overlapping institutionally with Goran Johansson, so I would not advocate B008 and would defer to others on it. My Lund background (Svanberg, Alden, the Lund Laser Centre) involves no collaboration with Katori or Ye. My alternatives B010 and B001 involve no personal tie to the named people.
